title: MyTm: An Automated Melting Temperature Calculation Toolkit
authors: Y. S. Huang, H. X. Song, Y. Sun, J. L. Li, Y. L. Xu, F. C. Wu, Y. C. Gan, Y. F. Wang, H. Wang, Hua Y. Geng
abstract: Melting temperature calculation is one of the important topics in computational materials science. In high-throughput in silico screening and artificial intelligence assisted design of materials, it usually requires a rapid and autonomous assessment of the melting temperature of the target. Unfortunately, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the melting point require many cumbersome and manual operations, making large-scale calculation of the melting point challenging. In this work, we introduce MyTm, a toolkit that employs MD to automatically determine the melting point. The method is fully modularized, and by combining these modules, the program enables fully automated melting calculations by using commonly adopted approaches, including the direct-heating method, the void method, the modified void method, the solid-liquid coexistence method, and the Z method. Moreover, a machine learning (ML) method is proposed and employed to recognize and classify the solid like and liquid like atoms, which effectively resolve the low accuracy issue in conventional classification approaches, thus making the automated high throughput pipeline of melting-point calculation possible. The robustness and efficacy of MyTm have been demonstrated by several well studied systems.
summary: This paper introduces MyTm, a fully automated toolkit designed to calculate the melting temperature of crystalline materials using Molecular Dynamics simulations. It modularizes the process, integrating multiple established MD techniques and crucially employs a Machine Learning classifier to accurately distinguish between solid-like and liquid-like atomic environments. This automation makes high-throughput screening of phase transitions significantly more feasible.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an automated, high-throughput computational method for accurately determining the melting temperature (Tm) of materials.
main_result: The proposed toolkit, MyTm, successfully automates various direct Molecular Dynamics (MD) approaches, yielding results comparable to literature values, especially using the solid-liquid coexistence method.
method: MyTm is a modular toolkit that integrates MD simulations with advanced atomic classification, including a Machine Learning (ML) component, to automate the complex process of phase transition calculation.
model_or_system: The toolkit is applicable to long-range ordered crystalline systems, simulating the solid-liquid phase transition using various models like perfect crystals, defective crystals, and two-phase solid-liquid coexistence models.
key_observables: Melting temperature (Tm), solid fraction, and thermodynamic quantities (Temperature, Pressure, Volume).
important_parameters: The choice of MD ensemble (NPT, NVE, etc.), solid/liquid cutoff thresholds, and simulation parameters are critical.
main_assumptions: The method is limited to crystalline solids and cannot handle amorphous materials; direct-heating and void methods are noted to overestimate Tm.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the constituent components of the calculation methods, the various models used (direct-heating, void, coexistence), and flowcharts detailing the temperature adjustment procedures.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the modular components of MyTm (model construction, ensemble selection, temperature control, classification), presents the ML enhancement, validates the method on several systems, and concludes with a comparison of results across different methods.
why_interesting: While focused on classical MD, the rigorous application of ML for phase identification and the development of a highly automated, modular framework for simulating complex phase transitions are relevant to developing robust computational tools for many-body dynamics.

Figure 3. Flowchart of the temperature adjustment procedures in MyTm. (a) Direct heating method: The program first verifies and adjusts whether the low and high temperatures correspond to the solid and liquid phases, respectively. It then performs MD simulations according to the heating rate and detects the melting point. (b) Bisection method: The program first checks and adjusts whether the low and high temperatures correspond to the solid and liquid phases, respec- tively, and then iteratively applies the bisection approach between the two phases to approximate the melting point.
